summary: Defines textual conventions for MIB modules that keep performance history in 15 minute intervals. It replaces RFC 2493, with changes noted in the module's revision clause. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Telecom equipment keeps its performance counters in quarter-hour slots. This document defines the shared names for the counters that fill those slots, so that any management tool can read a history of the last day and a half in the same way, whatever equipment it is talking to.

subtitle: Shared data types for MIB modules that keep statistics in 15-minute buckets.

tldr.problem: When a manager asks for a history of how a line has been behaving, each MIB module would otherwise invent its own way of storing and reporting that history.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines textual conventions: named types with a fixed syntax and precise meaning, so a module can reuse them. Three counter types cover the current interval, a stored interval and the total across intervals, plus objects for how long the current interval has run and how many intervals hold valid data.
tldr.outcome: A manager reads the same objects whatever module produced them, and knows when an interval is missing rather than reading a zero that means nothing. The document replaced RFC 2493 in 2003.

facts.label: Rotation at interval end
facts.value: IntervalCount(1) takes the value of CurrentCount

today: RFC 3593 is a Draft Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It replaced RFC 2493 in 2003, with the change limited to updated contact information and references and no technical changes, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The SONET/SDH managed objects in RFC 3592 are one of the modules that use these conventions.

sections.title: Buckets of Fifteen Minutes
sections.content:
When a manager wants a history of how some equipment has behaved, a MIB can be designed in several ways. The agent can count events continuously and let the manager build the history from successive readings of the counter. Or the agent can allocate the events to buckets, each covering a span of time. Telecommunications equipment often uses the second approach, and for that equipment it is common to keep the history in fifteen-minute intervals.

The memo does not compare the merits of the strategies. The differences include polling policy, the amount of management traffic between manager and agent, agent simplicity and how current the data is when the manager gets it. MIB designers are asked to consider those aspects when choosing a strategy. What the memo provides is the set of definitions to use in MIB modules that need history data based on fifteen-minute intervals.

The conventions defined here are based on 32-bit counts. For high-capacity performance history counts, the document points to separate work in progress.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ways to keep a history are common: count everything and let the manager work out the history, or sort the counts into fixed time slots. Telecom gear does the second, with slots of fifteen minutes, and this document defines the shared vocabulary for that.

sections.title: Proxies and Missing Data
sections.content:
In this document a proxy means an application that receives SNMP messages and replies to them on behalf of devices where the actual implementation sits, for example DS3/E3 interfaces. The proxy has already collected the information about those interfaces into its local database and may not necessarily forward requests to the actual interface.

It is expected that there are periods when the proxy is not communicating with the interfaces it represents. During those periods the proxy will not necessarily have up-to-date configuration information and will most likely have missed collecting some data. Missed data collection may result in some intervals in the interval table being unavailable, which is why the conventions include a way of saying how many intervals hold valid data and how many are missing.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy answers SNMP requests on behalf of equipment it watches. When it loses touch with that equipment it misses data, and the document says how to report the gaps instead of pretending the counters were zero.

sections.title: The Time Elapsed Object
sections.content:
Each measured entity is expected to have an object named after it, of the form xyzTimeElapsed, giving the number of seconds since the current measurement period began. The object has a maximum, but there are cases, such as an adjustment in the system's time-of-day clock, where the actual value of the current interval would exceed it.

The document works through the case of an agent that aligns its fifteen-minute measurement intervals to fifteen-minute time-of-day boundaries and has a clock that systematically gains time, which the manager periodically corrects by setting it back. Assuming the clock is reasonably accurate, say within a few seconds per day, the corrections will normally be small, and if they are made often enough they need never exceed ten seconds. In that case all interval durations stay within the allowed tolerance and none need be marked invalid, provided the procedure of ending measurement intervals at fifteen-minute time-of-day boundaries is followed.

If the clock is adjusted in small increments, always ending measurement intervals at those boundaries results, in the long term, in the correct number of intervals with the correct average duration, whether the clock is moved ahead or moved back. If the current interval does exceed the maximum, it is acceptable for the agent to return the maximum value.
sections.plainLanguage: One object says how far into the current quarter-hour we are. It has a ceiling, and the document explains that a clock adjusted a little at a time will not break the counting as long as the intervals still end on the quarter-hour.

sections.title: Valid and Invalid Intervals
sections.content:
Each measured entity is expected to have an object named xyzValidIntervals, giving the number of previous near-end intervals for which data was collected. The overall constraint on the number of intervals is 1 to 96, and any additional constraint has to be defined in the description of the object.

The value will be the full number of intervals unless the measurement was started or restarted within the last n times fifteen minutes, in which case it is the number of complete fifteen-minute intervals for which the agent has at least some data. In certain cases, such as a proxy, some intervals can be unavailable, and then this object holds the highest interval number for which data is available.

A companion object, xyzInvalidIntervals, counts the intervals in the range from 0 to xyzValidIntervals for which no data is available. It will typically be zero, except in cases where the data for some intervals is not available.
sections.plainLanguage: Two objects keep the bookkeeping honest: how many of the stored slots actually hold data, and how many are holes. A manager can then tell a missing interval from a quiet one.

sections.title: The Three Counter Conventions
sections.content:
PerfCurrentCount is a counter for a measurement in the current fifteen-minute interval. Its value starts at zero and rises as events occur, until the end of the interval. At that point the value is stored in the first history interval and the current count restarts at zero. If the agent has no valid data for the current interval, the object instance does not exist, and a request for it returns an error, for example noSuchName in SNMPv1 and noSuchInstance for an SNMPv2 GET.

PerfIntervalCount is a counter for a previous fifteen-minute interval, with the same rule about missing instances. In a system supporting a history of n intervals, where IntervalCount(1) is the most recent and IntervalCount(n) the least recent, the end of an interval does the following: the value of IntervalCount(n) is discarded, the value of IntervalCount(i) becomes that of IntervalCount(i-1) for n greater than or equal to i and greater than 1, the value of IntervalCount(1) becomes that of CurrentCount, and the total count, if supported, is adjusted.

PerfTotalCount is a counter for a measurement that aggregates the previous valid fifteen-minute intervals. Intervals for which no valid data was available are not counted. All three conventions use the syntax Gauge32.
sections.plainLanguage: Three counters make up a performance history: one for the quarter-hour in progress, one for each stored quarter-hour, and one running total. At the end of a quarter-hour the newest value is stored and the whole set shifts along, dropping the oldest.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This memo defines textual conventions for use in other MIB modules. The security issues for those MIB modules are addressed in the memos that define them, and this document does not add anything to them.
sections.plainLanguage: This document only names the counters. Anything about who may read or change them belongs to the memo that defines the module using them.

viz.caption: WHAT AN AGENT USING THESE CONVENTIONS MUST SUPPORT

items.title: Quarter-hour history counters
items.text: The agent supports history counters based on 15-minute intervals.

items.title: A history of n intervals
items.text: The agent can keep a history of n intervals, where n is at most 96.

items.title: Optional totals
items.text: The agent may also support counters that aggregate the history intervals.

items.title: Separate tables
items.text: The current interval, the history intervals and the total aggregates are kept in separate tables.

messages.label: STORE AND RESET
messages.note: At the end of the interval the current value is stored as IntervalCount(1) and the current count restarts at zero.

messages.label: SHIFT
messages.note: IntervalCount(1) takes the value of IntervalCount(2), and so on down the history.

messages.label: DISCARD
messages.note: The value of the oldest interval, IntervalCount(n), is discarded.
